claim: The study analyzed 472,449 peer review reports using text-analysis software to determine linguistic characteristics.
source: Here we report the results of a study in which text-analysis software was used to determine the linguistic characteristics of 472,449 peer review reports.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the sample size and methodology used in the study.

claim: Reviewer recommendation had the biggest impact on the linguistic characteristics of reports.
source: We found that reviewer recommendation had the biggest impact on the linguistic characteristics of reports, and that area of research, type of peer review and reviewer gender had little or no impact.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: Area of research had little or no impact on the linguistic characteristics of peer review reports.
source: We found that reviewer recommendation had the biggest impact on the linguistic characteristics of reports, and that area of research, type of peer review and reviewer gender had little or no impact.
evidence: This finding is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the results section.

claim: Type of peer review had little or no impact on the linguistic characteristics of peer review reports.

evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data analysis.

claim: Reviewer gender had little or no impact on the linguistic characteristics of peer review reports.
source: We found that reviewer recommendation had the biggest impact on the linguistic characteristics of reports, and that area of research, type of peer review and reviewer gender had little or no impact.

claim: The lack of influence of research area, type of review or reviewer gender on the linguistic characteristics is a sign of the robustness of peer review.

claim: Peer review shortcomings include gender bias and other less obvious forms of bias.

claim: Open peer review leads to longer reports compared to confidential peer review.
source: To date most research on the linguistic characteristics of peer review has focused on comparisons between different types of peer review, and it has been shown that open peer review (in which peer review reports and/or the names of reviewers are made public) leads to longer reports and a more positive emotional tone compared to confidential peer review (Bravo et al., 2019; Bornmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.
